sentences.label: Plans and calls
sentences.text: This part adds up its inputs with fixed weights: an international plan takes a typical customer's chance of leaving from about 1% to about 20%, and calls to customer service raise it steadily, each adding about the same, from about 1% at 0 to about 4% at 3 calls.

sentences.label: Usage
sentences.text: A higher night-time charge (about 1% at 6.13 to about 2% at 11.88 US dollars), more international minutes (about 1% at 7 to about 2% at 14 minutes) and a higher evening charge (about 1% at 11.76 to about 2% at 22.57 US dollars) raise it steadily, while more daytime minutes lower it steadily, from about 2% at 112 to about 1% at 249 minutes.

sentences.label: State
sentences.text: Through it, the state moves the chance from about 1% in West Virginia to about 5% in California, about 4% in Washington and about 3% in Montana, and down to under 1% in Hawaii, New Jersey, Vermont and Illinois (each of these states has 41 to 90 training customers; the full list is in the technical detail).

sentences.label: Smaller effects
sentences.text: A longer account raises it steadily and more evening minutes lower it steadily, a voice-mail plan lowers it and area code 510 raises it, each by less than a point, and night-time minutes move it in an uneven way, by less than a point.

This part reads the daytime charge, voice-mail messages and calls to customer service, and acts on 1390 of 4000 training customers, 305 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is below 1% without it and about 3% with it.

Through it, the daytime charge adds nothing until about 32.38 US dollars (between 27.52 and 53.01 US dollars for different customers), then raises the chance steadily: for a typical customer from about 1% at 19.07 to about 17% at 42.40 US dollars.
The charge raises the chance only for customers without voice-mail messages, in an uneven way: from about 1% to about 17% without them, while with them it stays at about 1%.

This part reads daytime minutes, the evening charge and two states, and acts on 1030 of 4000 training customers, 288 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 4% without it and about 13% with it.

Through it, daytime minutes add nothing until about 222 minutes (between 173 and 271 minutes for different customers), then raise the chance steadily, for a typical customer from about 1% at 112 to about 3% at 249 minutes.
The evening charge counts more with more than 180 daytime minutes, rising slowly at first, then faster: from about 1% to about 4%, against about 1% to about 2% with fewer.
For the typical customer it acts on, a customer in North Carolina has about 9% and one in Maryland about 15%, instead of about 13%.

This part reads customer-service calls, the daytime and evening charges and a few states: through it, calls raise the chance in an uneven way, adding only from about 4 calls upwards (for a typical such customer from about 1% to about 3%), and a daytime charge above about 26.35 US dollars lowers it in an uneven way (for a typical such customer from about 5% to about 3%).
The evening charge barely changes it, and the states it reads (Iowa, Alaska, Ohio and Texas) move it by less than a point.
